parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a dispatcher. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.

Hello, thanks for taking the time to talk with me today. To get started, which company do you work for, and could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you from start to finish?

I work at one of the drone operating companies that uses the platform's shared service. As a dispatcher, my day involves planning and running flights, including deciding which drone flies and along which way, and signing off a flight before it leaves. Several of us often plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight if needed.

Could you walk me through a concrete example of one flight from the moment you find out it needs to happen until it finishes—who hands the work to you, and who do you hand things off to along the way?
I don't know.
Let's break that down: how do you know what flights you need to plan when you start your shift, and how do you interact with the fleet technicians or the airspace desk?
I don't know.
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what made it so bad?

I worry when the authorities announce a sudden airspace closure or amend an existing one while my drones are already in the air. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.
Could you tell me about a specific day recently when several of those things happened at once—what actually occurred and how did you handle it?
I don't know.
When you are signing off a flight or monitoring it, what do you currently check by hand because you don't trust the systems or data you have?
I don't know.

When you mentioned that several of you often plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, how do you make sure you don't double-book a drone or a site, or run into other problems before signing off a flight?
I don't know.
When something does go wrong with a flight or a drone, what is the very first information you need to know right after it happens?
I don't know.
Thinking about a new service being built for your work, what are you most afraid it might do wrong or make harder for you?

I worry that software might be built to choose a drone or a way for us to fly, which goes against our company policy that software never does that. I also worry about the service running on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and that occasionally crashes.
Why does your company have the policy that software must never choose the drone or the route, and what do you look at when you make those choices yourself?
Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher. Our company policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us.
When you sign off a flight before it leaves, what needs to be true before you are allowed to sign it off?
I don't know.
